newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy police seize disk in Berlusconi bugging case.
newsitem.headline: Italy police seize disk in Berlusconi bugging case.

text.p: Italian police on Monday seized a computer disk in which an anonymous person claimed to have made a bugging device found in former prime minister Silvio Berlusconi's office, state television reported.
RAI television said that the floppy disk was sent to a Rome-based news agency by a man who said he was an electronics enthusiast who made recording devices.

The report said the sender saw media mogul Berlusconi display the matchbox-sized device on television and recognised one of his creations, allegedly commissioned by an unnamed deputy from the Lazio region about a month ago.
A lawyer for Berlusconi earlier made a formal complaint about the bug, whose discovery has caused uproar in Italy, while politicians prepared to debate the affair.
Lawyer Giuseppe De Luca deposited two pages of documents containing details of how the bug was found.

"The fact is very serious since, in my role as a parliamentarian, under article 68 of the constitution I cannot be subjected to eavesdropping of any sort without the prior approval of the Chamber of Deputies," Berlusconi wrote.

The leaders of the various parties in the centre-left coalition on Monday discussed the bugging issue with signs of disagreement on whether parliamentary debate should be limited to the bugging or amplified to discuss judicial activities.

Berlusconi, whose global business empire includes a controlling interest in Italy's three main private television stations, told a news conference in Rome on Friday that a sweep of his office had detected the bug on Wednesday.
The revelation sparked immediate outrage across the parliamentary divide.

Disgraced former Socialist prime minister Bettino Craxi meanwhile declared in a statement issued in Tunisia, where he is a fugitive, that the affair was merely the "latest link in a chain of illegality."
De Luca said Berlusconi had yet to hand over the bug, described by some experts as amateurish, and had "no specific suspicions in any particular direction" about who planted it.

Referring to the possibility of "deviant offshoots" of official bodies being responsible for the device, De Luca said it was inconceivable to think of "a serious institution violating a principle of democratic law."
Berlusconi has complained repeatedly that he is being victimised by Milan's elite "Clean Hands" pool of anti-corruption magistrates.
The media mogul is on trial in Milan for alleged bribes paid by his Fininvest empire to finance police in return for lenient audits. He denies the accusations.
